title: Chapter 63: Six Clockwork Men, Part 2 of 5: Rowan
html:
At the third bell the clerks put down their pens for a quarter of an hour, the way they did every morning, and stood up and stretched, and some of them went to the stoves to warm their hands, and some of them went out to the privy at the end of the corridor, and some of them just stood at the tall windows and looked out at the gray roofs.
Wren stayed at her desk. She did not want to stand at a window. She did not want anybody to look at her.
She had her head down over her copying, pretending to read it, when a shadow fell across the page.
She looked up.
Rowan Thorne was standing beside her desk.
He was tall. Taller than she had thought, sitting down. A thin, straight, pale young man of sixteen in the black coat of an Academy cadet, buttoned to the throat, with a white stock at his neck and his dark hair cut short and brushed flat. He had his sister's face. Wren had not seen it before, because she had only seen him across the Long Office, or across a yard, or with his head bent over his work. Now he was close, and she saw it. The same small straight nose. The same dark brows. The same small line between the brows, as if he had been frowning, a little, his whole life.
His eyes were red at the rims. He had not been crying. She was sure of that. He was the kind of boy who would not cry in the Long Office if the roof fell in. But he had not slept.
"Cadet Halloway," he said. His voice was stiff and formal, an Academy voice. "May I speak to you."
It was not a question. Wren got up from her stool.
"Of course."
He did not say anything for a moment. He stood there, very straight, with his hands behind his back in the Academy way, and looked at the copying on her desk, and not at her.
"That tune," he said at last. "The one you were humming."
"I'm sorry. I didn't know I was. I do it sometimes. I don't—"
"Where did you learn it?"
She looked at him.
"I don't know," she said. It was the truth. "I've always known it. Since I was small. Only those three notes. I don't know the rest."
Rowan's jaw moved, the way a jaw moves when somebody is biting down on something.
"My mother sang it," he said. "When I was small. Before she—" He stopped. "Before. In the nursery, at night. All of it. Not just three notes." He was quiet. "I don't remember much about her. I was seven. But I remember that. It goes up, and then it hangs, and then it comes down." He looked at her for the first time, straight. "I haven't heard it since. Not once. And then you sat there and—"
He stopped again.
Wren did not know what to say. So she did not say anything.
Rowan looked away, at the window. Outside, it was beginning to rain.
"You live in his house," he said. Not a question either. "The Inquisitor's. On Steeple Lane."
"Yes."
"You were there yesterday."
"Yes."
He was quiet for a long time. The clerks were drifting back to their desks round them, and the stools were scraping, and somebody at the far end of the room coughed. Rowan did not seem to notice any of it.
"Nobody will tell me anything," he said, very low. "Aunt Cressida says he died peacefully. The Inquisitor's note says he died at the third bell after noon, in his care, and the arrangements are made, and I'm to be at Saint Clement's on Sunday at the second bell. That's all it says." His voice did not shake. It went very flat instead, and very quiet. "Was he alone?"
Wren looked at him.
She thought of rule one. Not hers. The harvester's. The girl's. No lies between us. She had heard the girl say it to him once, on the step, in a low fierce voice. She did not know why she thought of it now.
She thought of Kross saying, in the dark at the bottom of the cellar stair: you are a very bad liar, Halloway.
"No," she said. "He wasn't alone."
Rowan's hands, behind his back, closed.
"Your sister was there," said Wren. "She'd been there all day. Since before the first bell. She sat by the bed and held his hand. She counted his breaths." She stopped. She made herself go on. "I wasn't in the room. I was on the stair. But the door was open. And at the end—"
She stopped again.
"At the end?" said Rowan. Very quietly.
"He was tapping," said Wren. "On her hand. He'd been tapping all day. And at the end he tapped all the way up to fourteen. Slowly. One, and then two, and then three. And she said—" Wren found her own throat had gone tight. "She said, That's the landing, Father. That's all of them. You can stop now. And he stopped."
Rowan did not move.
He stood there by her desk, very straight, with his hands behind his back and his face perfectly still, and looked at the rain on the window. He did not say anything for so long that Wren began to think he had not heard her.
Then he said, "The stairs."
"I don't—"
"At home. On Crown Walk. There are fourteen stairs from the hall to the first landing." His voice was very odd. "She counts them. She's counted them every day since she was nine. I used to laugh at her for it." He swallowed. "I never knew why she did it."
He was quiet.
"Thank you," he said at last, stiffly, to the window. "Cadet Halloway."
He turned and went back to his desk across the aisle and sat down and picked up his pen. Wren sat down too. She picked up her own pen. She dipped it in the ink and held it over the paper and did not write anything.
Across the aisle, Rowan Thorne was not writing either. He was sitting with his pen in his hand, very still, looking at nothing. And then, as she watched, he put down the pen, and took a scrap of paper from the pile at the corner of his desk, and began to fold it. In half. In half again. Small and tight and hard, the way Kross folded things.
Wren looked away before he reached eleven.
The Card
Kross came in at the fourth bell, as he had said he would.
Wren heard the door at the near end of the Long Office open and shut, and the pens did not stop, because the pens never stopped for Kross. That was one of the things she had learned in two years. Other masters wanted the room to go quiet when they walked through it. Kross wanted it not to notice him. And so it did not. The pens went on scratching, and the clerks kept their heads down, and he walked the whole long length of the room between the two rows of desks without anyone looking up, a thin gray figure in a gray coat with his hat in his hand.
But Wren looked up. She could not help it.
He had changed his clothes. He had shaved. His hair was combed again, flat and neat and graying at the sides. He was buttoned to the throat in his plain dark Inquisitor's coat, with no braid on it and no badge, only a small silver pin at the collar in the shape of an open hand. His gloves were on. He looked exactly as he looked every morning.
Except for his eyes. She saw them as he passed her desk. They were red at the rims, and very tired, and they did not look at her, or at anything, but went straight ahead to his own door at the end of the room as if it were a long way off.
He went into his glass office and shut the door. A moment later the green lamp came on behind the glass.
Wren went back to her copying.
She copied for an hour. Names. Names. A woman taken at the Lower Docks for an unpaid memory debt, a childhood owed and not delivered. A man found in the river under Lantern Bridge, no name, gray to the elbows, a harvester, unlicensed. Deceased. Two children brought to the Intake Hall by the Health, brother and sister, no parents listed. Held. She copied them all in her small clean black hand and blotted them and laid them on the pile.
At the fifth bell a runner came.
He was a boy of twelve or so, in the gray tunic of the Ministry runners, with a satchel over his shoulder and a cold red nose. He came down the aisle between the desks quickly, looking at the numbers on them, and stopped at hers.
"Cadet Halloway?"
"Yes."
He held out a card. A small white card, folded once, sealed with a dab of gray wax with no mark in it. She took it. The boy went away again down the aisle without waiting.
She turned the card over. On the front, in a hand she did not know, square and careful and very upright, was her name. Cadet W. Halloway. By hand.
She broke the gray wax with her thumbnail and unfolded it.
Inside, in the same hand, there were only a few words.
The cellars under the Records yard. The third bell after noon. Come alone. Wear your coat.
There was no name at the bottom. There was nothing at all at the bottom.
Wren looked at it for a long time.
She did not know the hand. She knew most of the hands in the Ministry by now, the ones that came across her desk. This was not one of them. It was a careful hand. Not a clerk's. Clerks wrote fast and joined their letters. This hand did not join its letters at all. Each one stood on its own, separate, square, as if it had been made very slowly by someone who did not want to be mistaken.
She looked up at the glass office at the end of the room.
Kross was sitting at his desk behind the glass, under the green lamp. He was not writing. He was not reading. He was sitting very still with his gloved hands folded on the desk in front of him, looking at them.
Then, as she watched, he unfolded his hands, and took something small and white out of his waistcoat pocket. A peppermint paper. He unwrapped the sweet and put it in his mouth. Then he began to fold the paper, slowly, on the desk in front of him. In half. In half again. In half again.
Wren counted without meaning to. Kross's folds were famous in the Long Office. The clerks made jokes about them, very quietly, when he was out. How many today?
Six. Seven. Eight.
Nine. Ten.
Eleven.
He pressed the small hard square flat with his thumb, and put it back in his waistcoat pocket.
Then he looked up, through the glass, straight at her.
She dropped her eyes to her desk at once. Her face went hot. When she dared to look up again, a long moment later, he was writing, his head bent, as if he had never looked up at all.
She folded the card. Not eleven times. Twice. And put it inside her coat, in the left breast pocket, where she kept her small book.
Then she went back to her copying, and at the second bell after noon, when the clerks went down to the long cold room in the basement for their bread and soup, she did not go with them. She sat at her desk and watched the clock above the door at the near end of the Long Office move, very slowly, toward the third bell.
At the quarter before it, she got up and put on her coat.
The Empty Desk
She went the long way down.
She did not mean to. There was a short way from the Long Office to the Records yard, down the main stair and along the ground-floor corridor and out by the clerks' door, and she had walked it a hundred times. But when she came out of the Long Office into the corridor with her coat on, her feet turned the other way, toward the back of the building, toward the narrow stair that went up to the third floor, and she let them.
She knew why. She did not say it to herself.
The third floor at the back of the Ministry was the Harvesting Section. It was a smaller room than the Long Office, and darker, and colder, with only two windows, both looking out at the blank wall of the Records yard. Six desks stood in it, in two rows of three. There was a stove in the corner that nobody seemed to have lit. There was a rack of silver rods on the wall by the door, in a glass-fronted case, locked. There was a smell, faint, sweet and burnt, like sugar left too long on a stove, that the clerks said never quite went out of the walls, however often the room was aired.
She stopped in the doorway.
Five of the desks had things on them. Ink, pens, papers, a cup, a scarf thrown over a stool. People's things. People who would come back from their bread and soup in a quarter of an hour and sit down.
The sixth desk, in the far corner by the cold window, had nothing on it at all.
It had been cleared. Not tidied. Cleared. The top of it was bare wood, scrubbed, with pale squares on it where things had stood for years and kept the light off. The drawer was out. It was lying upside down on the floor beside the desk, empty, where somebody had pulled it out and turned it over and shaken it and dropped it. The stool had been taken away. There was only the desk, and the upside-down drawer, and the pale squares.
Wren knew whose desk it was. She had seen it once before, in the autumn, when she came up here with a message for him from Kross, and he had been sitting at it with his head in his hands and a jar of something blue on the corner, and had looked up at her with eyes that did not quite know who she was.
"He's not coming back, is he."
She turned.
There was a young man sitting at one of the other desks. She had not seen him, because he was sitting very low, hunched over, behind a pile of folders. He had red hair, very red, sticking up at the crown, and a round face covered in freckles, and he was holding a bun in one hand. He had been eating it. He was not eating it now. He was looking at her, at her white coat and her twelve silver buttons, with an expression she knew very well: the expression of a clerk who has just realized he has said something out loud to the Inquisition that he should not have.
He went red. Redder. All the freckles disappeared.
"Sorry," he said. "Sorry, Cadet. I didn't—I wasn't—"
"It's all right."
"I just meant—" He looked at the bun in his hand as if he did not know how it had got there. "It's on the list. His name. I saw it on the board. To be held on sight." He swallowed. "He used to leave me his crusts. On the corner of the desk. Every day. He didn't like crusts. I did." He stopped. "Sorry."
Wren looked at him.
She knew who he was. She had heard about him this morning, in the Long Office, from Sedley at the next desk, who had heard it from a porter. A clerk from Harvesting, yesterday, had hung his coat over the brass Ash lamp above the Records yard doors, for no reason anybody could think of, and stood beside it in his shirtsleeves in the cold for a quarter of an hour, and then taken it down again. And an hour after he took it down, the lamp had gone white, all by itself, as if something with Ash in it had passed under it while nobody was looking. Red hair, the porter had said. Freckles. Always eating. Daft as a brush.
She had guessed, then, who had walked under that lamp. She had said nothing to anybody. She had not even written it in her book.
"What's your name?" she said.
The young man looked as if he might be sick.
"Toby," he said. "Junior clerk. Harvesting. Cadet."
"Toby." She looked at the empty desk, and the drawer upside down on the floor. "He's alive. He's gone north."
Toby stared at her.
She should not have said it. She knew it as she said it. It was not a secret, exactly. Ferrand knew it, and the Archon knew it, and the card had said it: a man with gray hands, by the dyke road, going north. By tonight half the Ministry would know it. But she had not been told to say it. She had not been told to say anything. And she had said it to a junior clerk with a bun in his hand, because he had looked at an empty desk the way she had looked at a cold cup of tea on a stair.
"North," said Toby.
"Yes."
He looked at the bun. Then he put it down very carefully on a folder, as if it were something precious.
"Thank you," he said.
Wren did not answer. She turned and went back down the narrow stair, fast, and along the corridor, and down to the Records yard. And all the way, she thought about the drawer lying upside down on the floor, empty, and about a jar of something blue that had stood on the corner of a desk, and about the fact that she had now told two people the truth in one day, without being asked to by anyone. Rowan Thorne. And a red-haired clerk called Toby.
She did not think she was a very good cadet, today.
Down
The Records yard was at the back of the Ministry, on the river side, and it was the ugliest place Wren knew.
It was a square of black cobbles, wet always, even in a frost, because the river damp came up through the stones. High gray walls stood round it on all four sides, five floors of them, with small barred windows in rows, so that standing in the middle of the yard was like standing at the bottom of a well. A cart ramp went down at one end, steep and slimy, to a pair of big iron loading doors set into the base of the wall. Over the doors, on an iron bracket, hung a brass Ash lamp, burning its hard blue-white light all day and all night, so that the wet cobbles under it shone blue and nobody who went in or out could do it without walking through the light.
Wren walked through it. She felt nothing, as she always felt nothing. She had no Ash in her. The lamp stayed blue and steady over her head.
There was a cart in the yard.
It stood by the far wall, out of the rain under a small slate roof that jutted from the wall on iron brackets, with no horses in its shafts. A black carriage, closed, with a little barred window high in its side. Wren knew it. Everybody on the river side of the city knew it. On its door there was a seal, painted in blue: a round seal, with a white open hand in the middle of it, and round the edge, in gold letters, THE MINISTRY. OFFICE OF PUBLIC HEALTH. FOR THE CARE OF THE CITY.
The Friday cart. It went out from here every Friday morning, early, to the Fish Stairs and the Lower Docks and the arches, and came back every Friday afternoon. It had come back already today. She could smell it from across the yard, even in the rain. Peppermint.
Two men were standing beside it. Not drivers. Workmen, in canvas aprons, with a ladder, and two pots at their feet, and a long flat board leaning against the cart's wheel. The board had letters cut out of it. A stencil. Wren could not read the letters from where she stood. The men were not doing anything. They were standing with their hands in their apron pockets, looking at the painted seal on the cart door, the way workmen look at a wall they have been told to paint over and have not yet been told what color.
One of them saw her looking, and looked away.
She did not know why it made her uneasy. It was only a cart. Only paint. Under-Secretary Pallister had burned in the Bourse on Midwinter Night, and the whole city knew by now that his Office of Public Health had been feeding Lull to the slum children and selling what came out of them. Of course they would paint over his seal. Of course they would want a new name on the door.
She only wondered, crossing the wet black cobbles under the blue light toward the iron door, what the new name would be.
At the bottom of the ramp, to the left of the loading doors, there was a smaller door. A plain one, of black iron, with no handle on the outside. A man in a gray Inquisition coat stood beside it with his hands behind his back. She did not know him. He looked at her coat, and at her face, and then he knocked on the iron door with his knuckles, twice and then three times, the same pattern she used on Moll's door, and the door opened inward, and he stood aside.
She went in.
A stair went down.
It was a stone stair, very old, worn into a dip in the middle of each step by hundreds of years of feet, and it went down and round and down and round in a tight spiral, with an iron rope fixed to the wall to hold on to and an oil lamp in a cage every twenty steps or so. Wren went down it with her hand on the cold iron rope. The air got colder as she went. Colder, and damper, and it began to smell. Of river mud, first. Then of oil. Then of something else, sharp and metallic, like the inside of a mouth when you have bitten your tongue.
Iron filings, she thought, after a while. That's what it is. Iron, and oil, and old wet stone.
She counted the steps without meaning to. She thought of the girl, Lyra, who counted everything. Sixty-one. Sixty-two. At eighty, the stair stopped turning and went straight down for a little way, and then stopped altogether at a door.
It was an old door, of oak gone black, bound with iron, and it stood open.
Beyond it was the cellar.
Wren had not known there was a place like this under the Ministry. She had worked in the building for two years. She had been down to the basement where the clerks ate, and to the cells under the Watch wing, and once, on an errand for Kross, to the record stores, where the old ledgers were kept in damp rows on wooden racks. She had not known there was anything under those. She had not known that under the basements and the cells and the stores there was this.
It was a vault. A brick vault, long and low, with a curved ceiling of old red brick gone black with soot and damp, and the curve of it came down on both sides to meet the floor, so that it was like being inside a tunnel, or the belly of a great brick fish. It was long. As long as a street. Longer than the Long Office upstairs. She could not see the far end of it. Oil lamps hung from iron hooks along the middle of the ceiling, one every ten paces or so, each in its own iron cage, and they made pools of yellow light on the floor below them, one after another, going away into the dark, with darkness between them, like the stepping stones across a river at night.
The floor was brick too. It was wet. Little channels had been cut in it, running to drains, and the water ran in them, very quietly.
And in the first pools of light, near the door, there were six long crates.
They stood on trestles, in a row, side by side, a little way apart. Each one was long and narrow, as long as a man, and a little wider than a man's shoulders, and made of rough new pine boards nailed together, with rope handles at the ends. Each one had a lid. The lids were down. Stenciled on the end of each crate, in black, there was a word, and the word was the same on all six.
FRAGILE.
Wren stopped just inside the door.
She could not have said why. They were only crates. She had seen a thousand crates. The Intake Hall was full of crates; the docks were full of them; half the things that came and went from the Ministry came and went in crates.
But these were the size and shape of coffins. And they stood on trestles, side by side, in the yellow light, the way coffins stand in a church before a funeral. And she had watched a coffin carried down a stair that morning, under a black cloth.
She made herself walk forward.
There was someone standing at the far end of the row of crates, in the edge of the last pool of light. An old man. She had not seen him at first, because he was so still, and so bent, and dressed in such dark clothes, that he looked like part of the shadows.
He was looking at the crates. He had not heard her come in. Or he had heard her and did not care.
As she came closer she heard that he was talking. Very low, under his breath, in a soft, cracked, steady voice. Not to her. Not to anyone she could see.
To the crates.
"There now," he was saying. "There now. It's cold, I know. It's a cold place. Not long now. Not long."
